title: Specificity-Aware Diffusion Steering via Variance-Reduced Sequential Monte Carlo

paper.title: Specificity-Aware Diffusion Steering via Variance-Reduced Sequential Monte Carlo
paper.abstract:
Abstract Inference-time steering enables pretrained diffusion models to satisfy new constraints without full retraining. However, specificity-aware generation is difficult: repelling samples from a negative reference distribution can also erode the positive distribution where the two overlap. The key challenge is to suppress negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution.
We address this problem by formulating specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem and deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective. The resulting target keeps the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired reference distribution, giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity. To sample from the corresponding time-dependent target path, we develop a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal. We further introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure with the Jacobian–vector products with the desired and undesired score fields. Experiments on synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image tasks and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder show that the proposed method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing the SMC weight collapse compared with negative-guidance baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/WangLuran/Specificity-Aware-Diffusion-Steering

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and score-based models have become standard tools for high-dimensional generation [ 1 , 2 ] . One important advantage of these models is that their sampling process can be steered at inference time, without retraining the underlying models [ 3 ] [ 4 ] . This makes them suitable for settings where generation must satisfy both positive and negative constraints: samples should remain close to a desired distribution while avoiding regions associated with an undesired reference distribution. [ 5 ] Existing steering methods, including classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance, negative prompting, and safe-generation guidance, modify the denoising direction or score estimate to promote or suppress selected attributes [ 6 ] [ 7 , 8 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] . However, these methods usually define a steering rule rather than an explicit target distribution. As a result, when the desired and undesired densities overlap, repulsive guidance can suppress valid modes and induce mode shift. [ 11 ] [ 12 ] [ 13 ] [ 14 ] To address this issue, we formulate specificity-aware diffusion steering. We introduce a specificity-aware target distribution that preserves the desired density only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired density. To sample from the resulting time-dependent target path, we use Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC). SMC provides a distributionally principled mechanism for diffusion steering through propagation and reweighting [ 15 ] [ 16 ] [ 17 ] . However, its stability depends on the variance of incremental weights [ 18 ] . We therefore derive a local proposal rule using forward–backward Gaussian kernel ratios, following the density-ratio view of guided diffusion [ 19 ] . The backward drift is chosen to cancel the leading fluctuation in the log-weight, and the remaining leading-order terms define a tractable variance objective for adapting the proposal. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate negative guidance as sampling from a specificity-aware target distribution derived from an overlap-based objective, yielding a principled likelihood-ratio gate that preserves positive mass while suppressing negative overlap. Second, we develop a proposal-aware SMC sampler with a gate-augmented forward kernel and locally optimized backward kernel to reduce diffusion-path weight degeneracy. Third, we introduce a fixed-noise optimization procedure using retained-order weight surrogates and Jacobian–vector products to optimize ESS without retraining the base model. We validate the method on synthetic dataset, class-contrastive generation, and Stable Diffusion text-to-image benchmarks with both related and unrelated negative prompts as well as the peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder design. Across these settings, our method reduces mode shift, improves sampling stability, and better removes negative concepts than the baselines while preserving positive-prompt quality.

sections.heading: Diffusion guidance and negative guidance.
sections.text: Diffusion and score-based generative models can be steered at inference time by modifying their reverse-time score, denoising direction, or velocity field without retraining the base model [ 20 , 1 , 2 ] . Such guidance can use classifiers, rewards, or compositions of learned score and flow fields [ 6 , 7 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Negative guidance further suppresses undesired concepts during sampling [ 8 , 9 , 25 , 10 ] . However, these methods typically define the resulting distribution only implicitly, and repulsive updates can remove valid modes when desired and undesired concepts overlap. In contrast, we define an explicit specificity-aware target that preserves probability mass favored by the desired reference while penalizing regions more characteristic of the undesired reference, and derive a sampler for its diffusion path.

sections.heading: Feynman–Kac correction and density-ratio steering.
sections.text: Feynman–Kac and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate target distributions through propagation, reweighting, and resampling [ 15 , 16 ] . Recent work applies these ideas to diffusion guidance and model composition [ 17 ] , as well as test-time sampling from reward-modified targets [ 26 ] . Density-ratio approaches instead characterize diffusion control through local transition-kernel ratios, avoiding explicit estimation of higher-order PDE quantities [ 19 ] . We adopt this forward–backward kernel-ratio view for proposal design and use local kernel ratios to reduce the variance of incremental SMC weights.

sections.heading: SMC stability and proposal optimization.
sections.text: A central difficulty in SMC is weight degeneracy, which reduces effective sample size and can destabilize guided sampling [ 15 , 16 ] . Prior work has improved SMC proposals through proposal tuning, importance weight optimization, path-space objectives, optimal-control formulations, annealing schedules, prior shifts, and timestep adaptation [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] . These methods often fix part of the underlying dynamics, optimize within a restricted proposal family, or focus primarily on schedule adaptation. Our approach instead jointly analyzes the local forward and backward Gaussian kernels to construct low-variance proposals.

sections.heading: pMHC-specific binder design.
sections.text: Peptide–MHC (pMHC) targeting is a challenging specificity problem because different targets largely share the same MHC scaffold, while specificity is often determined by only a few exposed peptide residues. Earlier TCR-mimic antibody design preserved MHC interactions while redesigning peptide-contacting residues [ 35 ] . More recent generative approaches have designed peptide-focused pMHC binders using explicit off-target filtering, in silico cross-panning, and large-scale off-target screening [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] . These approaches are closely related to classical negative design, which favors the desired interaction while penalizing competing states [ 39 ] . Our work instead studies pMHC specificity through inference-time guidance of a pretrained binder generative model. Figure 1 : Comparison of target distributions in two one-dimensional examples. Blue and orange denote the desired density p A p^{A} and undesired density p B p^{B} , respectively; green denotes the induced target. The proposed target preserves regions where p A p^{A} dominates p B p^{B} and removes regions with high undesired density. By contrast, DNG can shift mass away from desired modes, while the negative-prompt (NP) construction does not consistently suppress the undesired region.

At the continuous level, after matching the target path and control family, our matched drift induces the same Feynman–Kac potential as the corresponding DriftLite-VCG control [ 34 ] . Its potential-variance objective is the leading-order coefficient of the second term above. Our finite Gaussian construction instead evaluates the realized one-step weight, retaining the quadratic trace estimator and the additional finite-displacement corrections. The benefit is therefore in the finite-step weight construction and optimization objective, rather than in separate continuous control principles. This also connects to DAS [ 26 ] : for a fixed forward kernel, its ideal backward proposal minimizes the conditional transition variance. Our coefficients additionally modify the forward kernel together with its matched backward proposal. sections.heading: 5.1 Synthetic Specificity on a 40-Component Gaussian Mixture
sections.text: Figure 2 : Visualization on the 40-MoG synthetic task. The task setting contains A A -only target modes, B B -only negative modes, and A ∩ B A\cap B suppressed modes. The target distribution retains only the A A -only modes. In the first experiment, the 40-MoG synthetic dataset [ 17 ] [ 19 ] is used to evaluate class-contrastive sampling. As shown in Fig. 2 , the 40 Gaussian modes are randomly divided into three groups: A A -only modes, B B -only modes, and overlapping A ∩ B A\cap B modes. The desired target distribution retains the A A -only modes while suppressing both the B B -only and A ∩ B A\cap B modes. The proposed sampler produces samples that are visually closest to the target distribution. Dynamic Negative Guidance (DNG) [ 10 ] suppresses several negative regions, but it also induces mode shifts, especially for the modes in the lower-right region. Negative Guidance fails to represent the target distribution accurately and retains substantial mass near negative regions. SSafe Denoiser (SD) [ 25 ] removes the negative modes more effectively than Negative Guidance, but its repulsion is driven by the absolute B B -density. Consequently, it can over-repel samples from regions where B B is dense, causing missing or weakened positive modes that are surrounded by or close to negative modes, such as those in the lower-left region. This supports the use of a ratio-based gate, which activates repulsion according to the relative evidence p B / p A p_{B}/p_{A} rather than the absolute negative density alone.

sections.heading: 5.4 Specificity-Aware pMHC Binder Design
sections.text: We evaluate our method on a protein-design task that requires specificity between two closely related targets. The desired target is an HLA-A*02:01– β 2 \beta_{2} m complex presenting NLVPMVATV . The undesired target has the same HLA-A*02:01– β 2 \beta_{2} m scaffold but presents NLVFMVATV . The peptides differ only at position 4, where Pro in the desired target is replaced by Phe in the undesired target. Thus, successful discrimination must depend on the presented peptide rather than on a change in the MHC scaffold. We design an 80 80 -residue binder using the desired pMHC as the positive condition and the undesired pMHC as the negative condition. The candidate and propagated weights use the same retained Proposition 2 expansion. The complete target construction, weight terms, clipping rules, and hyperparameters are given in Appendix F . We use eight matched to generate 64 candidate binders. We then retain one inverse-folded sequence per backbone. Generation uses 200 200 reverse-diffusion steps. Each sequence is modeled with both the desired and undesired pMHC using Boltz-2.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented a specificity-aware diffusion steering framework that preserves a desired distribution while suppressing an undesired one. We first derive an explicit target from an overlap-based objective. Its softened likelihood-ratio gate retains regions specific to the desired distribution without inducing the global mode shift of standard negative guidance. We then construct an SMC sampler that locally minimizes the empirical relative variance of cumulative surrogate weights using the full displacement and one score Jacobian–vector product per reference model. Experiments on synthetic 40-MoG, CIFAR-10, text-to-image generation, and pMHC binder design show improved target fidelity, specificity, and particle diversity. The framework is distributionally grounded, training-free, and applicable when desired and undesired reference models are available.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations
sections.text: Our method assumes stochastic SDE inference and a local one-step approximation; extending it to deterministic solvers, EDM parameterizations, and finite-time flow maps is left for future work. It also introduces application-specific hyperparameters and additional compute from particle sampling with two reference models. Evaluation is limited by the lack of a large-scale text-to-image specificity benchmark. For binder design, we study only one peptide pair with a modest number of candidates, and assess specificity using predicted iPTM rather than experimental affinity. Larger-scale studies with experimental on- and off-target validation are needed.

sections.text: Fig. 6 reports the Wrong %–KL Pareto for the forward direction for completeness; the method ordering is consistent with the Recall plot in the main text. We prefer Recall over KL in multiclass selection for two reasons. First, KL to uniform over | 𝒦 | = 3 |\mathcal{K}|=3 keep classes has only three histogram bins, so it measures class-level balance but is blind to intra-class diversity: a method can attain KL ≈ 0 \mathrm{KL}\approx 0 while collapsing each kept class to a single stereotypical mode (e.g. the full variety of airplane views to a single canonical pose), and this mode shaving is invisible. Recall instead uses 15,000 15{,}000 reference points in 2048 2048 -dimensional InceptionV3 feature space with the standard k k -NN manifold construction, so each real image votes independently on whether its local neighbourhood is covered, and boundary-adjacent modes lost under blanket guidance (e.g. unusual horse poses, dark-background frogs close in score space to the suppressed cat class) show up directly as a Recall drop. The nine-bin histogram of class removal has enough resolution to compensate; at | 𝒦 | = 3 |\mathcal{K}|=3 it does not. Second, the evaluate.py KL computation uses unnormalised keep-class fractions (it divides by total sample count rather than renormalising over keep classes), so the raw KL inherits a log ⁡ ( 1 / ( 1 − W ) ) \log\!\bigl(1/(1-W)\bigr) artefact that is monotone in Wrong %; the number can be corrected post hoc, but Recall has no such ambiguity. sections.heading: F.1 Task Setting
sections.text: We study specificity-aware protein-binder design for two closely related peptide–MHC class I complexes. The desired target is HLA-A*02:01– NLVPMVATV , whereas the undesired target is HLA-A*02:01– NLVFMVATV . The two peptides differ only by a Pro-to-Phe substitution at peptide position 4. Their normalized T-cell activation values in the BATCAVE mutational-scan dataset are 1.000 1.000 and 0.031 0.031 , respectively. These measurements are used only to select a biologically relevant specificity pair and are not treated as affinity labels for the generated binders. Both targets contain the same HLA-A*02:01 heavy chain and β 2 \beta_{2} -microglobulin. The generated object is an 80 80 -residue protein binder, denoted by chain X X . The conditioning target contains the HLA heavy chain, β 2 \beta_{2} -microglobulin, and the nine-residue peptide; no T-cell receptor is included. Peptide residues 3–6, which include the mutated position, define the intended binding region, while β 2 \beta_{2} -microglobulin is marked as non-binding.

sections.heading: F.2 Construction of the Paired Targets
sections.text: The desired and undesired pMHC structures are initially predicted with Boltz-2. The undesired complex is aligned to the desired complex using a Kabsch fit on the HLA platform, defined by the C α \alpha atoms of HLA residues 1–180. We then construct an exact shared molecular context by copying the desired HLA and β 2 \beta_{2} -microglobulin coordinates into both conditions, while retaining the corresponding desired or mutated peptide. Consequently, the two inputs share the same presentation scaffold and differ only in the peptide sequence and peptide conformation. During generation, a Kabsch fit on the same HLA platform removes the small numerical frame drift between the two conditional denoiser evaluations. Across the reported Proposition 2 generation, the median fitted rotation over the final low-noise quarter of sampling is 0.029 ∘ 0.029^{\circ} , and the maximum across backbone particles is 0.179 ∘ 0.179^{\circ} . Thus, the contrastive field is not dominated by an arbitrary rigid-body mismatch.

sections.heading: Interpretation.
sections.text: These results show that likelihood-ratio gating with an adaptive two-field proposal and Proposition 2 weight propagation can shift the center of the generated-binder distribution toward stronger predicted recognition of the desired peptide relative to a single-residue off-target. The reported ipTM margin is a structural interface-confidence surrogate and should not be interpreted as a calibrated binding affinity. Experimental binding and off-target measurements remain necessary to validate the generated specificity.

However, specificity-aware generation is difficult: repelling samples from a negative reference distribution can also erode the positive distribution where the two overlap. The key challenge is to suppress negative mass while minimally distorting the positive distribution. We address this problem by formulating specificity-aware steering as a target-design problem and deriving a target distribution from an overlap-based objective. The resulting target keeps the desired reference distribution only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired reference distribution, giving a likelihood-ratio interpretation of specificity. To sample from the corresponding time-dependent target path, we develop a Sequential Monte Carlo sampler with a variance-minimized local proposal. We further introduce a practical fixed-noise optimization procedure with the Jacobian–vector products with the desired and undesired score fields. Experiments on synthetic task, class-contrastive generation, text-to-image tasks and peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder show that the proposed method suppresses undesired regions more effectively, reduces mode shift, and improves sampling stability by decreasing the SMC weight collapse compared with negative-guidance baselines. Code is available at: https://github.com/WangLuran/Specificity-Aware-Diffusion-Steering 1 Introduction Diffusion and score-based models have become standard tools for high-dimensional generation [ 1 , 2 ] . One important advantage of these models is that their sampling process can be steered at inference time, without retraining the underlying models [ 3 ] [ 4 ] . This makes them suitable for settings where generation must satisfy both positive and negative constraints: samples should remain close to a desired distribution while avoiding regions associated with an undesired reference distribution. [ 5 ] Existing steering methods, including classifier guidance, classifier-free guidance, negative prompting, and safe-generation guidance, modify the denoising direction or score estimate to promote or suppress selected attributes [ 6 ] [ 7 , 8 ] [ 9 ] [ 10 ] . However, these methods usually define a steering rule rather than an explicit target distribution. As a result, when the desired and undesired densities overlap, repulsive guidance can suppress valid modes and induce mode shift. [ 11 ] [ 12 ] [ 13 ] [ 14 ] To address this issue, we formulate specificity-aware diffusion steering. We introduce a specificity-aware target distribution that preserves the desired density only in regions where it is sufficiently preferred over the undesired density. To sample from the resulting time-dependent target path, we use Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC). SMC provides a distributionally principled mechanism for diffusion steering through propagation and reweighting [ 15 ] [ 16 ] [ 17 ] . However, its stability depends on the variance of incremental weights [ 18 ] . We therefore derive a local proposal rule using forward–backward Gaussian kernel ratios, following the density-ratio view of guided diffusion [ 19 ] . The backward drift is chosen to cancel the leading fluctuation in the log-weight, and the remaining leading-order terms define a tractable variance objective for adapting the proposal. Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate negative guidance as sampling from a specificity-aware target distribution derived from an overlap-based objective, yielding a principled likelihood-ratio gate that preserves positive mass while suppressing negative overlap. Second, we develop a proposal-aware SMC sampler with a gate-augmented forward kernel and locally optimized backward kernel to reduce diffusion-path weight degeneracy. Third, we introduce a fixed-noise optimization procedure using retained-order weight surrogates and Jacobian–vector products to optimize ESS without retraining the base model. We validate the method on synthetic dataset, class-contrastive generation, and Stable Diffusion text-to-image benchmarks with both related and unrelated negative prompts as well as the peptide-MHC (p-MHC) binder design. Across these settings, our method reduces mode shift, improves sampling stability, and better removes negative concepts than the baselines while preserving positive-prompt quality. 2 Related Work Diffusion guidance and negative guidance. Diffusion and score-based generative models can be steered at inference time by modifying their reverse-time score, denoising direction, or velocity field without retraining the base model [ 20 , 1 , 2 ] . Such guidance can use classifiers, rewards, or compositions of learned score and flow fields [ 6 , 7 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Negative guidance further suppresses undesired concepts during sampling [ 8 , 9 , 25 , 10 ] . However, these methods typically define the resulting distribution only implicitly, and repulsive updates can remove valid modes when desired and undesired concepts overlap. In contrast, we define an explicit specificity-aware target that preserves probability mass favored by the desired reference while penalizing regions more characteristic of the undesired reference, and derive a sampler for its diffusion path. Feynman–Kac correction and density-ratio steering. Feynman–Kac and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods approximate target distributions through propagation, reweighting, and resampling [ 15 , 16 ] . Recent work applies these ideas to diffusion guidance and model composition [ 17 ] , as well as test-time sampling from reward-modified targets [ 26 ] . Density-ratio approaches instead characterize diffusion control through local transition-kernel ratios, avoiding explicit estimation of higher-order PDE quantities [ 19 ] . We adopt this forward–backward kernel-ratio view for proposal design and use local kernel ratios to reduce the variance of incremental SMC weights. SMC stability and proposal optimization. A central difficulty in SMC is weight degeneracy, which reduces effective sample size and can destabilize guided sampling [ 15 , 16 ] . Prior work has improved SMC proposals through proposal tuning, importance weight optimization, path-space objectives, optimal-control formulations, annealing schedules, prior shifts, and timestep adaptation [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] . These methods often fix part of the underlying dynamics, optimize within a restricted proposal family, or focus primarily on schedule adaptation. Our approach instead jointly analyzes the local forward and backward Gaussian kernels to construct low-variance proposals. pMHC-specific binder design. Peptide–MHC (pMHC) targeting is a challenging specificity problem because different targets largely share the same MHC scaffold, while specificity is often determined by only a few exposed peptide residues. Earlier TCR-mimic antibody design preserved MHC interactions while redesigning peptide-contacting residues [ 35 ] . More recent generative approaches have designed peptide-focused pMHC binders using explicit off-target filtering, in silico cross-panning, and large-scale off-target screening [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] . These approaches are closely related to classical negative design, which favors the desired interaction while penalizing competing states [ 39 ] . (b) Undesired pMHC presenting NLVFMVATV . 6 Conclusion We presented a specificity-aware diffusion steering framework that preserves a desired distribution while suppressing an undesired one. We first derive an explicit target from an overlap-based objective. Its softened likelihood-ratio gate retains regions specific to the desired distribution without inducing the global mode shift of standard negative guidance. We then construct an SMC sampler that locally minimizes the empirical relative variance of cumulative surrogate weights using the full displacement and one score Jacobian–vector product per reference model. Experiments on synthetic 40-MoG, CIFAR-10, text-to-image generation, and pMHC binder design show improved target fidelity, specificity, and particle diversity. The framework is distributionally grounded, training-free, and applicable when desired and undesired reference models are available. 7 Limitations Our method assumes stochastic SDE inference and a local one-step approximation; extending it to deterministic solvers, EDM parameterizations, and finite-time flow maps is left for future work. It also introduces application-specific hyperparameters and additional compute from particle sampling with two reference models. Evaluation is limited by the lack of a large-scale text-to-image specificity benchmark. For binder design, we study only one peptide pair with a modest number of candidates, and assess specificity using predicted iPTM rather than experimental affinity.
